dialogue.speaker: Nurse · Prenatal clinic
dialogue.text: Hi, I’m calling from your prenatal clinic. WIC may help pay for groceries during your pregnancy.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: If I qualify, am I already signed up?

dialogue.speaker: Nurse · Prenatal clinic
dialogue.text: No. You still need to enroll with WIC.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Okay. What do I need to do?

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Who do I contact first?

dialogue.speaker: WIC staff
dialogue.text: Contact your local WIC office. We’ll explain the appointment and what information to provide.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: So this is more than filling out a form.

dialogue.speaker: WIC staff
dialogue.text: Yes. We review eligibility and complete a nutrition assessment before issuing benefits.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: I already have Medi-Cal. Does that count?

dialogue.speaker: WIC staff
dialogue.text: That can establish income eligibility. We still need to complete your WIC assessment.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Being connected to one program doesn’t automatically connect me to this one.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: My baby is here. Do my benefits stay the same?

dialogue.speaker: WIC staff
dialogue.text: Your package changes after birth and depends on your feeding circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: In this example, I’m fully breastfeeding. I’ll check the updated food balance before shopping.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Can I use it at my usual store?

dialogue.speaker: WIC app · store finder
dialogue.text: Check for a WIC-authorized store. This Smart & Final is listed by California.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: This example route is 2.7 miles. The starting point is illustrative—not a real participant’s home.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: A card does not guarantee a nearby store. This national finding is separate from our example route.

dialogue.speaker: Mom · thinking
dialogue.text: Let’s start with milk. Which kind matches my balance?

dialogue.speaker: WIC app
dialogue.text: For this package: approved 1% low-fat or nonfat milk. There are 4 gallons available.

dialogue.speaker: Mom · thinking
dialogue.text: White eggs or brown eggs? They look so similar.

dialogue.speaker: WIC app
dialogue.text: Check the approved type and size. The right product matters as well as the food category.

dialogue.speaker: Mom · thinking
dialogue.text: Bread, peanut butter, apples, peas. One item at a time.

dialogue.speaker: Mom · thinking
dialogue.text: And dish soap. That will be on my part of the bill.

dialogue.speaker: Cashier · illustrative
dialogue.text: WIC covered these foods. The dish soap is $3.49.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: The groceries haven’t changed. But I pay $3.49 instead of $22.63.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: What would that add up to?

dialogue.speaker: Illustrative calculation
dialogue.text: One purchase like this each month would mean $229.68 less household spending over a year.

era: Early infancy · back in the kitchen

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: These are the groceries from this trip.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: WIC paid for the foods with blue labels. I paid for the soap.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: There are other groceries at home already. This trip didn’t buy them.

dialogue.speaker: WIC balance
dialogue.text: The full package contains more than this purchase. Unused allowances stay on the balance—not in the cabinet.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: I bought these groceries. What’s still available?

dialogue.speaker: WIC balance
dialogue.text: 3 gallons of milk. 1 dozen eggs. 28 ounces of whole grains. $49.12 for produce.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: And the foods I haven’t bought yet are still on the balance.

dialogue.speaker: WIC balance
dialogue.text: Use benefits within their issue period. Check the first and last day to use them.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Does everyone use everything they receive?

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: This study measured how much of each food category people used during a certification period.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: 69.6% of periods with produce benefits reached at least 70% use. That does not mean 69.6% of all produce dollars were used.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: So getting the benefit and using it are different things.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: There’s another appointment. Is this the same as renewing?

dialogue.speaker: WIC staff
dialogue.text: A mid-certification assessment is different from renewal. We’ll tell you what information needs updating.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Now she’s one. Her package changes again.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: At two, we’re still buying groceries—and keeping up with WIC.

dialogue.speaker: Illustrative calculation
dialogue.text: Across 48 monthly purchases, this fixed basket would cost the household $918.72 more without WIC.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: How many eligible families are missing this support?

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: WIC reached 56.1% of all eligible people in an average month in 2023.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: It reached 82.3% of eligible infants, but only 26.9% of eligible four-year-olds.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: These are different age groups. The chart does not measure this family leaving WIC.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Would this look different in another state?

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: California reached 72.4% of eligible people. Louisiana reached 41.3%—a 31.1-percentage-point gap.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: Vermont’s estimate is 79.6%, but its interval is wide: 65.1%–94.2%.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: The ranking doesn’t tell us why. Store access, referrals and logistics need their own evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Does staying connected make a difference beyond the grocery bill?

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: A study found a 3.6-point lower diet-quality score among children participating only in their first year.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: Higher scores mean better diet quality. This was an adjusted, observational comparison—not proof of cause and effect.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: Could getting this help take less work?

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: Electronic benefits replaced paper vouchers. A national study associated that change with increased child participation.

dialogue.speaker: Research context
dialogue.text: Better referrals and easier renewal are operational changes to evaluate—not effects measured by that electronic-benefit study.

dialogue.speaker: Mom
dialogue.text: The list comes back next week. I need the support to keep working, too.
